header.contentArea: Perioperative care: postoperative complications (observations, bloods and CT released in stages)
guidelineVersions: NICE NG253 Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over (Nov 2025, updated Sep 2026)
WSES intra-abdominal infections guideline (Sartelli et al., 2017)
Sawyer et al., N Engl J Med (2015)

related.why: Referring a septic postoperative patient to the registrar by SBAR, with fluid and antibiotic detail

brief.scenario: Mr Neville Ashdown, 68, had an emergency Hartmann's procedure for perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with purulent peritonitis. On the evening of day 1 the nurse calls you because his temperature is 38.2°C.
brief.task: The examiner will give you his observations, results and imaging in stages. Interpret each and tell the examiner what you would do.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: A temperature is a reason to assess the patient. Look for the source, grade the risk, act on it.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Naming 'day 1 atelectasis' or a calendar mnemonic instead of examining him.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "I'd go and see him: full set of observations, NEWS2, then examine from chest to calves."

grid.label: Assess the patient, not the number
grid.fail: Calls day-1 fever atelectasis, or starts antibiotics, without seeing him.
grid.pass: Sees him: observations and NEWS2, chest, abdomen, wound, stoma, lines, urine output, calves, drug and transfusion charts.
grid.high: Says atelectasis has not been shown to cause fever; early fever is often inflammatory. Sets repeat observations and a clear re-review trigger.

grid.label: Differential by source
grid.fail: Recites a day-by-day mnemonic as the diagnosis.
grid.pass: Lists by source: chest, urine, wound, line, intra-abdominal collection, VTE, drug or transfusion reaction.
grid.high: Ties it to this operation: pelvic abscess or rectal stump leak; uses timing only to weight likelihood, never to exclude.

grid.label: Recognise sepsis (safety-critical)
grid.fail: Treats day-6 fever and tachycardia as routine; no NEWS2, no escalation.
grid.pass: NEWS2 7 with suspected infection: high risk. Senior review; venous gas with lactate, cultures; broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and IV fluid bolus within 1 hour.
grid.high: Gives 250 ml boluses over 10–15 minutes, reassessing after each, up to 1,000 ml; catheter, hourly urine output; outreach if not improving.

grid.label: Interpret the bloods
grid.fail: Reads the CRP alone, or misses the creatinine rise.
grid.pass: Rising white count and CRP after an earlier fall, raised lactate and acute kidney injury: a septic complication.
grid.high: Notes no anastomosis after a Hartmann's; the trend matters: a second rise is a complication (stump leak or collection) until proven otherwise.

grid.label: Choose the right imaging
grid.fail: Requests only an abdominal X-ray or ultrasound, or waits until tomorrow.
grid.pass: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast today, once resuscitated; discusses the kidney injury with radiology rather than delaying.
grid.high: Asks radiology whether rectal contrast would help assess the rectal stump.

grid.label: Interpret the CT and source control
grid.fail: Plans antibiotics alone for a large pelvic abscess in a septic patient.
grid.pass: Pelvic abscess by the rectal stump: image-guided percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics; pus sent for culture.
grid.high: Relaparotomy if not drainable, generalised peritonitis or no improvement; short antibiotic course once source control is adequate.

grid.label: Escalate and communicate
grid.fail: Does not inform the registrar or tell the patient what is happening.
grid.pass: Informs the registrar in a structured way, documents, and explains the concern and plan to the patient and nurse.
grid.high: Agrees a time for senior review and explicit triggers for critical care; is honest that a complication is suspected.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Day 1. Temperature 38.2°C. What do you think?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's day 1, so it's atelectasis. I'd ask for chest physio and start antibiotics to be safe.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Wind on day 1, water on day 3, wound on day 5, walking on day 7.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: Day 6. Temperature 38.7, pulse 114, BP 102/64, RR 23, SpO2 94% on air.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: Probably a wound infection. I'd swab it and see him on the ward round.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: The CRP is high, so infection.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: CT shows a 6 cm pelvic collection with gas.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd continue antibiotics and repeat the scan in a week.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd hand it over in the morning.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Day 1. Temperature 38.2°C. What do you think?

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: I'd go and see him. Full observations and NEWS2, then examine chest, abdomen, wound, stoma, cannula sites and calves, check urine output, and look at the drug and transfusion charts.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A source: chest, urine, wound, line, an intra-abdominal collection, VTE, or a drug or transfusion reaction.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Day 6. Temperature 38.7, pulse 114, BP 102/64, RR 23, SpO2 94% on air, alert.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: That's a NEWS2 of 7 with suspected infection, so high risk. I'd get senior review, do a venous blood gas with lactate and take blood cultures, and give broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and an IV fluid bolus within the hour.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: Bloods: CRP 290, it was 110 on day 4. White cells 19.4, creatinine 138 from 82, lactate 2.6.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Inflammatory markers are rising again, lactate is up and he has an acute kidney injury. This is a septic complication until proven otherwise.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast today, once resuscitated. I'd discuss the kidney injury with radiology rather than delay.

pass.speaker: examiner
pass.text: CT: 6 cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection with gas beside the rectal stump.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A pelvic abscess. I'd ask for image-guided percutaneous drainage, continue antibiotics and send the pus for culture.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The registrar now, in a structured call. I'd document and explain to Mr Ashdown and his nurse what we think is happening.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Day 1. Temperature 38.2°C. Observations otherwise normal. Chest clear, wound clean.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Early fever after a laparotomy for peritonitis is often inflammatory. Atelectasis hasn't been shown to cause fever, so I won't label it that. I'd ask for four-hourly observations and to be called if NEWS2 rises.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: Which cause worries you most in him?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: After a Hartmann's for pus, a pelvic abscess or a rectal stump leak. Timing only shifts likelihood; it never rules anything out.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: High risk. The fluid goes in as 250 ml boluses over 10 to 15 minutes, reassessing after each, up to 1,000 ml in total. A catheter for hourly urine, and critical care outreach if he doesn't respond.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: His CRP on day 3 was 150 and fell on day 4. Now it's 290.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: He has no anastomosis after a Hartmann's, so the trend is what matters: it fell and has now risen again. A second rise is a complication until proven otherwise, here a rectal stump leak or a pelvic collection.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd ask radiology whether rectal contrast would help show the stump.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Relaparotomy, or sooner if he develops generalised peritonitis or doesn't improve. Once source control is adequate, a short course of about four days of antibiotics is enough.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The registrar is in theatre for an hour.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: I'd agree when they'll see him and involve outreach now if he stays high risk. And I'd tell Mr Ashdown honestly that we think there's a collection and what we plan to do.

failures.move: Treating day-6 fever and tachycardia as a wound problem for the morning round.
failures.consequence: Delays antibiotics and source control in a patient at high risk of death from sepsis.

failures.move: Diagnosing atelectasis from the calendar without examining him.
failures.consequence: Misses a treatable source and gives unneeded antibiotics.

failures.move: Antibiotics alone for a large abscess in a septic patient.
failures.consequence: Without drainage the sepsis persists; he deteriorates.

failures.move: Requesting an abdominal X-ray and waiting.
failures.consequence: Cannot show a collection; delays the CT that decides management.

recovery.line: I wouldn't assume that. I'd examine him and look for a source, because atelectasis hasn't been shown to cause fever.
Then I'd treat the physiology: he is high risk, so senior review now and repeat imaging or intervention guided by the registrar.

knowledge.fact: Atelectasis has not been shown to cause postoperative fever.
NEWS2 of 7 or more with suspected infection is high risk: broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within 1 hour.
High risk: IV fluid bolus within 1 hour; 250 ml over 10–15 minutes, reassess after each, up to 1,000 ml total.
Well-defined abscesses: percutaneous drainage plus antibiotics; surgery if not drainable or peritonitis.
After adequate source control, about 4 days of antibiotics was as good as longer courses.

recall.think: Sepsis from a pelvic abscess or leak.

sources.name: NICE NG253. Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management

sources.name: Mavros MN, Velmahos GC, Falagas ME. Atelectasis as a cause of postoperative fever: where is the clinical evidence? Chest 2011;140:418-24
sources.supports: No clinical evidence that atelectasis causes early postoperative fever

sources.supports: About 4 days of antibiotics after adequate source control was non-inferior to longer courses

media.task: Calculate NEWS2 and identify the deterioration
media.description: NEWS2 observation chart for days 1 to 6 showing a day-1 temperature spike that settles, then rising temperature, pulse and respiratory rate on day 6

media.task: Describe the abnormality and plan source control
media.description: Axial contrast-enhanced CT of the pelvis showing a rim-enhancing gas-containing collection beside a stapled rectal stump

partner.opening: Mr Ashdown is on day 1 after a Hartmann's procedure for purulent peritonitis. His temperature is 38.2°C. What would you do?

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks for observations or examines (stage 1, day 1)
reveals.finding: T 38.2°C, HR 96, BP 128/76, RR 18, SpO2 97% on air, alert. NEWS2 2. Chest clear. Abdomen tender around the wound only. Wound clean. Stoma pink. Urine 50 ml/h. Cannula site clean. Calves soft. No transfusion.
T 38.7°C, HR 114, BP 102/64, RR 23, SpO2 94% on air, alert (NEWS2 7). Lower abdominal pain; stoma output has dropped. Wound slightly red, no discharge. Chest clear. Urine 20 ml/h for 2 hours.
WCC 19.4. CRP 290 mg/L (150 on day 3, 110 on day 4). Creatinine 138 µmol/L (baseline 82). Venous lactate 2.6 mmol/L. Blood cultures sent.
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast: 6 cm rim-enhancing pelvic collection containing gas, beside the rectal stump. No free intraperitoneal gas. Stoma enhancing normally.

push.question: Is day-1 fever atelectasis?
push.expect: No: not proven to cause fever; examine and look for a source.

push.question: What causes fever after surgery?
push.expect: By source: chest, urine, wound, line, collection or leak, VTE, drug or transfusion reaction.

push.question: What is his NEWS2 on day 6 and what does it mean?
push.expect: 7: high risk; senior review; venous gas with lactate, cultures; IV antibiotics and fluid bolus within 1 hour.

push.question: Interpret the bloods.
push.expect: Second rise in CRP and white count, raised lactate, AKI: septic complication.

push.question: What imaging and when?
push.expect: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast today.

push.question: How will you treat the collection?
push.expect: Image-guided drainage plus antibiotics; relaparotomy if not drainable or peritonitic.

push.question: Who do you tell?
push.expect: Registrar now; patient and nurse; documented plan and triggers.

curveballs.prompt: Suppose he had spiked a fever during a blood transfusion on the ward.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Stop the transfusion if still running, check the patient and unit identity, observations, and follow the transfusion reaction protocol.

curveballs.prompt: The radiologist cannot drain it: it is behind loops of bowel.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Discuss with the consultant: consider transrectal/transgluteal access or relaparotomy; continue antibiotics.

curveballs.prompt: His NEWS2 is still 7 an hour after antibiotics and fluid.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Escalate to the registrar and critical care outreach now.

curveballs.prompt: What is the role of lactate?
curveballs.safeAnswer: It helps grade severity and response to treatment; a normal lactate does not exclude sepsis.
